scope: Exact worker-authored method and conclusion excerpts; not independent adequacy grades or pooled effect estimates. Different region definitions and inference methods remain distinct.

method_and_conclusion_excerpts.quote: The supplied maps do **not** support a positive gain effect in vmPFC after whole-brain correction. In the primary one-sample test, 11 voxels survived one-sided Bonferroni family-wise error correction across 186,400 brain-mask voxels, but none overlapped the vmPFC mask; the strongest voxel was posterior (MNI −26, −102, −3.6 mm; *t*(53) = 6.62; corrected *p* = .0017). A participant sign-flip maximum-statistic sensitivity analysis found no whole-brain corrected voxels. The original NARPS instructions required whole-brain corrected results for the named hypothesis, rather than an ROI-only decision ([instructions](https://www.narps.info/files/narps_instructions_for_analysis_teams.pdf); [NARPS study report](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2314-9)).

Within an independently defined vmPFC mask, the mean participant gain coefficient was −0.0078 (95% CI −0.0343 to 0.0187; 23/54 participant means were positive). This descriptive estimate is near zero and its interval includes zero. It is not a separate corrected test. The positive whole-brain voxels were posterior and do not localize to the hypothesized region.

*Figure 1. Unthresholded one-sample t statistics in the x≈0 sagittal slice. Yellow outline is bilateral AAL3v2 Frontal_Med_Orb, the atlas-defined vmPFC area. No voxel in this mask survived whole-brain correction. The displayed slice is for localization, not a separate statistical test.*

All 54 listed equal-indifference participants were included. The maps had matching dimensions and affine transforms and finite values. The search mask was the intersection of voxels with nonzero values in every cope map and the MNI152 brain mask resampled to the supplied MNI152NLin2009cAsym grid (186,400 voxels). No participant had a brain-wide mean or standard-deviation QC score beyond |z| = 3; no exclusions were made.

We tested whether the population mean cope was greater than zero at each voxel with a one-sample *t* test (54 participants; 53 df; one-sided). Bonferroni correction across the entire search mask controls family-wise error without relying on spatial smoothness. The strongest positive statistic was *t* = 6.62, one-sided uncorrected *p* = 9.31×10⁻⁹ and Bonferroni *p* = .00174; 11 voxels passed the corrected threshold, none within vmPFC. As a sensitivity analysis, we used 9,999 participant-level sign flips and a maximum studentized statistic across all tested voxels; this found no voxels at FWE *p* ≤ .05. The two correction approaches differ in posterior voxels, but neither provides corrected evidence in vmPFC.

vmPFC was localized independently from the observed activation using the bilateral AAL3v2 `Frontal_Med_Orb` labels. This anatomically specific label is used as vmPFC in the AAL3 literature ([Rolls et al., 2020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31521825/); [OFC atlas definitions](https://www.oxcns.org/papers/620%20Hsu%20Rolls%20et%20al%202020%20Connections%20of%20the%20Human%20Orbitofrontal%20Cortex.pdf)). We used the anatomical mask to identify whether corrected whole-brain results fell in the hypothesized region, not to replace the required whole-brain correction with an ROI test.

Participant variance maps were not supplied. The group model consequently gives each participant equal weight and estimates uncertainty from between-participant variation; it cannot reproduce an inverse-variance mixed-effects analysis or propagate first-level variance estimates. The conventional *t* model assumes independent participants and an adequately behaved sampling distribution. The sign-flip sensitivity instead relies on symmetry of participant effects under the null and was more conservative here. The posterior Bonferroni voxels lie near the edge of the search mask, so they should not be taken as substantive evidence for the target hypothesis.

The supplied gain-effect estimates do **not support a positive vmPFC response to potential gain** in the equal-indifference group. In an a priori 12 mm sphere centered at MNI (0, 40, -12), the mean participant effect was -0.0057 model units (95% CI [-0.0323, 0.0210]); the one-sided group test was *t*(53) = -0.43, *p* = .664. No voxel in the sphere survived whole-brain correction. A positive conclusion is not warranted by the small posterior signal found elsewhere in the brain.

We analyzed all 54 participant contrast parameter estimates in a one-sample, positive-direction group model. The model estimates the average participant effect with equal participant weights: participant variance maps were unavailable, so precision-weighted mixed-effects inference could not be fit. We used the source-reported MNI152NLin2009cAsym brain mask (TemplateFlow, resampled to the image grid) intersected with voxels having finite, nonzero map support in at least 90% of participants (192,333 voxels). There were no exclusions. Image checksums, sizes, IDs, and grids matched the supplied manifest; no participant had an absolute robust z-score above 3 for their mean over the analysis mask.

The primary voxelwise test was a one-sided one-sample Student *t* test with Bonferroni familywise correction over the full analysis mask. Bonferroni controls familywise error regardless of spatial dependence, at the cost of power, and the voxelwise *t* test assumes approximately Gaussian participant effects. Eleven posterior voxels survived this threshold (*t* cutoff 5.71); the peak was at MNI (-26, -102, -3.6), *t* = 6.62, Bonferroni-adjusted *p* = .0018. These voxels are well outside the vmPFC ROI and do not support the target hypothesis.

As a sensitivity analysis, we also used 4,999 one-sided sign-flip permutations of the one-sample *t* statistic and compared the observed maximum with the whole-brain maximum-*t* null. No voxel survived this correction (minimum corrected *p* = 1.00; 95th percentile null maximum *t* = 39.39). The unusually large null maximum indicates unstable extremes in voxelwise studentized statistics; this sensitivity is more conservative than the parametric Bonferroni test. The vmPFC result is null under both approaches. The exact random seed is 20261015.

Because “vmPFC” has no single universally agreed boundary, we operationalized it before examining group results as a 12 mm-radius sphere centered at MNI (0, 40, -12): a midline, anterior, ventral prefrontal location. The whole-brain corrected map remains the inferential family; ROI localization does not replace or relax that correction. The center is marked in the mean-effect figure, and participant-level sphere averages are shown below.

The original NARPS instruction states the positive vmPFC gain hypothesis for the equal-indifference group and asks teams to use whole-brain corrected inference ([NARPS analysis instructions, Hypothesis 1](https://www.narps.info/files/narps_instructions_for_analysis_teams.pdf)).
![Whole-brain Bonferroni-corrected positive t map. The surviving posterior voxels are outside vmPFC.](wholebrain_bonferroni_fwe.png)
![Participant-level vmPFC sphere-average effect estimates and 95% confidence interval.](vmPFC_participants.png)

The supplied maps do **not** support a positive gain-related response in vmPFC at the required whole-brain family-wise error (FWER) threshold. No vmPFC voxel passed correction. The descriptive vmPFC estimate was slightly negative, with a confidence interval that includes zero; this is inconclusive about a small positive effect, not evidence that the true effect is absent.

We analyzed all 54 equal-indifference participants using the supplied AO86 gain-effect maps. Checks confirmed that participant IDs matched the maps, all images shared a grid, all values were finite, and every map's SHA-256 matched `input/sources.json`. No participants were excluded. The search mask comprised 210,968 voxels present (nonzero) in at least 49 of 54 maps, limiting inconsistent edge coverage.

At each voxel we tested whether the group mean cope was positive with a one-sample t statistic. Whole-brain inference used 9,999 participant-level sign-flip permutations and the maximum positive t across the full search mask on each permutation (one-sided max-T; FWER α=.05). This controls voxelwise family-wise error across the whole brain and directly evaluates the directional hypothesis. The sign-flip test assumes participant estimates are independent and exchangeable under a symmetric null. The primary results were 24 corrected voxels in three small 26-connected components, all in posterior occipital cortex; the largest component peaked at MNI [-26, -102, -3.6] mm (t=6.62, max-T p=.0007). These locations do not support the vmPFC hypothesis.

To make vmPFC localization explicit without replacing the whole-brain test with an ROI test, we defined an anatomical sphere of 10-mm radius centered at MNI [0, 42, -8] mm, covering anterior medial orbitofrontal/vmPFC. The sphere was set independently of the group map and used for localization and descriptive summaries only. Its participant-averaged estimate was -0.0095 map units (SD=.103; 95% t interval [-0.0377, 0.0187]); the most positive voxel in the sphere had max-T adjusted p=1.00. The whole-brain corrected regions and the sphere are shown in Figure 1; Figure 2 shows the participant-level ROI values.
![Mean gain-effect estimates, with whole-brain corrected voxels outlined in black and the vmPFC sphere in gold.](figures/group_mean_vmPFC.png)
![Participant-level mean estimates in the vmPFC sphere.](figures/vmPFC_subject_estimates.png)

The analysis is limited to ordinary group inference on the supplied estimates: participant-level variance maps were unavailable, so first-level uncertainty could not be incorporated through precision weighting or a full hierarchical model. The sign-flip test also depends on symmetry of the participant-level null distribution. Failure to detect a vmPFC effect means this analysis did not find the hypothesized positive response under this group model and whole-brain correction; it does not demonstrate a zero effect, rule out a smaller effect, or establish that vmPFC does not represent gain.

# Potential gain and brain activity in the NARPS equal-indifference group

Does the participant-level gain effect increase in vmPFC? In this group-level analysis, **we found no whole-brain-corrected evidence for a positive vmPFC response**. None of the 24 voxels passing one-sided whole-brain correction overlapped our anatomically defined vmPFC approximation. The ROI-average coefficient was near zero (mean −0.0011 arbitrary model units; 95% t interval −0.0228 to 0.0207). This is a failure to find corrected support for the hypothesis, not evidence that the true response is exactly zero.

The input was the complete set of 54 AO86 participant gain-effect maps for the equal-indifference group in MNI152NLin2009cAsym space. We tested the group mean coefficient against zero at each voxel using a one-sample t statistic, with a one-sided positive alternative. Inference used 5,000 synchronized participant-level sign flips (seed 20261015). For each flip, we retained the largest positive t over the whole analysis mask. The resulting maximum-t distribution controls voxelwise family-wise error at 0.05 across the whole brain; the observed critical value was **t = 5.36**. This studentized sign-flip test treats participants as the sampling units and does not require a parametric spatial smoothness model. It does assume participant effects are exchangeable under the null (approximately symmetric about zero). The cluster table reports connected components of voxels passing voxelwise correction; cluster extent was not itself the correction statistic.

The mask is the intersection of nonzero estimation support across all 54 maps (198,029 voxels; 1,901 ml). Zeros outside an individual's estimation mask were therefore not interpreted as zero effects. We used the Harvard-Oxford cortical max-probability atlas at its 25% threshold as an anatomical localization aid. Our transparent vmPFC approximation combines Frontal Medial, Subcallosal, Frontal Orbital, and Paracingulate labels, restricted to |MNI x| ≤ 20 mm, y ≥ 0 mm, and z ≤ 0 mm, then intersects that region with the group mask (2,203 voxels). There is no agreed anatomical boundary for vmPFC; this atlas-based approximation is not identical to the original NARPS paper's combination of Harvard-Oxford regions and a Neurosynth map. We used whole-brain corrected inference for the hypothesis and report ROI summaries descriptively.

These are group tests of supplied participant coefficient maps, not re-estimates from time series. In the equal-indifference group, the range of potential gains was twice the range of potential losses. The fixed upstream model mean-centered and variance-normalized the gain regressor before HRF convolution; a coefficient is therefore not change in BOLD per currency unit. Upstream effects were averaged across four runs; gain and loss were modeled separately, so this analysis does not compare their slopes. No participant-level variance maps were supplied, so the group analysis cannot use precision-weighted mixed-effects estimates or propagate uncertainty from each participant's first-level model.

All 54 maps passed SHA-256 verification against `input/sources.json`, had finite values, and shared the same spatial grid. No participant was excluded. Whole-brain correction identified 24 positive voxels in three small posterior clusters. The peak was **t = 6.62**, whole-brain FWE **p = 0.0008**, at MNI **(−26, −102, −3.6)**; no corrected cluster overlapped the vmPFC approximation. This posterior finding is outside the hypothesized region and does not support Hypothesis 1.

The vmPFC approximation's mean across participants was −0.0011 (SD 0.0796; 95% t interval −0.0228 to 0.0207); 25/54 participant ROI means were positive. The strongest voxel in the ROI had **t = 4.19**, whole-brain FWE **p = 0.788**. The one-sample ROI summary and its interval are descriptive and do not replace the required whole-brain-corrected test.

## Interpretation and limitations

The data do not provide whole-brain-corrected support for increased vmPFC activity with potential gain in this group. The interval remains compatible with small positive or negative mean coefficients, and this analysis was not an equivalence test. Thus, lack of support does not show that vmPFC is unresponsive, that potential gain has no behavioral value, or that the effect is absent under another model or contrast. N=54, first-level measurement error is unavailable, and the upstream gain coefficient reflects a normalized regressor in a separate gain model. The vmPFC approximation is necessarily operational; a different defensible boundary could change the ROI summary, while the whole-brain corrected test avoids relying on that boundary for its primary conclusion.
- Corrected clusters: [`fwe_clusters.tsv`](fwe_clusters.tsv)
- Participant ROI means: [`vmPFC_participant_means.tsv`](vmPFC_participant_means.tsv)
- NIfTI outputs: mean coefficient, SD, t, whole-brain FWE p, corrected mask, group support mask, and vmPFC approximation mask in this directory.

The original NARPS instructions specify a positive vmPFC effect for Hypothesis 1 and the equal-indifference group ([instructions PDF](https://www.narps.info/files/narps_instructions_for_analysis_teams.pdf)). The NARPS report describes the lack of a single agreed vmPFC boundary and its use of atlas plus Neurosynth information ([NARPS paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2314-9)). The atlas labels were obtained through Nilearn's [Harvard-Oxford dataset interface](https://nilearn.github.io/stable/modules/datasets.html).

The supplied gain-effect maps do **not support a positive vmPFC response to increasing potential gain** in the equal-indifference group under the required whole-brain corrected test. The largest statistic in the independently defined vmPFC region was small (t = 1.30; whole-brain max-t FWE p = 1.00). The average vmPFC effect estimate was slightly negative, and its 95% confidence interval included zero. Positive whole-brain corrected effects occurred in small posterior/inferior clusters outside vmPFC; those findings do not support the stated vmPFC hypothesis.

We analyzed all 54 supplied AO86 participant gain-effect maps in the equal-indifference group. Input file size and SHA-256 checksums were verified against `input/sources.json`. All maps had matching 97 × 115 × 81 grids, 2 × 2 × 2.4 mm voxels, and finite values. No participant was excluded. The group mask was the intersection of nonzero voxels in all 54 maps (198,029 voxels), so background zeros outside any participant's modeled coverage were not treated as observations.

The primary model was an intercept-only one-sample group model of participant effect estimates, testing the positive direction. We used 10,000 permutations (seed 20261015) and voxelwise maximum-t family-wise error correction across the full common brain mask (alpha = .05). This provides whole-brain rather than ROI-only correction, consistent with the [NARPS analysis instructions](https://www.narps.info/files/narps_instructions_for_analysis_teams.pdf). The permutation one-sample test assumes effects are symmetrically distributed about zero under the null; the correction uses the maximum t statistic across the analysis mask ([Nilearn documentation](https://nilearn.github.io/0.14.0/modules/generated/nilearn.glm.second_level.non_parametric_inference.html)).

We defined vmPFC independently as a 10 mm radius sphere centered at MNI [0, 46, -6], a commonly used value-related vmPFC location informed by meta-analysis ([Bartra et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3756836/); see also [Dore et al., 2016](https://brucedore.github.io/Dore_et_al_JOCN_2016.pdf)). The sphere included 413 voxels in the shared mask. It was used to localize the target region; the inferential support criterion remained voxelwise whole-brain FWE p < .05.

The vmPFC sphere's mean participant effect was -0.011 (between-participant SD = 0.108; 95% t interval for the mean [-0.041, 0.018]). Its maximum statistic was t = 1.30 at [0, 42, -8.4] MNI, with whole-brain max-t FWE p = 1.00. No voxel in the vmPFC sphere passed whole-brain correction.

Across the full brain, 24 voxels in three 26-connected clusters passed positive-direction max-t FWE correction. The global maximum was t = 6.62 at [-26, -102, -3.6] MNI (FWE p = .0009). All corrected foci were outside the vmPFC sphere. The anatomical label and biological interpretation of these small posterior/inferior foci are not central to the vmPFC hypothesis and should be treated cautiously.

![Positive whole-brain effects surviving voxelwise max-t FWE correction; cyan marks the vmPFC center](results/figures/whole_brain_fwe_map.png)

The maps are participant contrast parameter estimates, not standardized statistics or group-level results. The gain regressor was mean-centered and variance-normalized before HRF convolution, so its coefficient is not a change per currency unit. The response regressor used response-time durations; gain and loss were fit in separate models. Consequently, the estimate is conditional on those fixed upstream choices. No participant variance maps or complete executable upstream pipeline were supplied, so we could not perform precision-weighted group inference or re-estimate the first-level model. The group model gives participants equal weight. The subject-level permutation inference relies on a symmetric null distribution, and its p-values should be interpreted within the defined mask and tested positive direction.

The supplied maps do **not support** a positive gain effect in vmPFC under whole-brain family-wise error (FWE) control. In 54 equal-indifference participants, no voxel in the prespecified vmPFC search zone survived one-sided permutation max-statistic correction (9,999 sign flips; minimum attainable p = .0001). The largest positive statistic inside that zone was *t*(53) = 4.19 at MNI [-2, 24, -18] mm, but its whole-brain FWE *p* was .778. The mean participant effect averaged over the search zone was -0.00010 (95% *t* interval [-0.01434, 0.01414], in upstream coefficient units).

Across the brain mask, 24 voxels passed FWE *p* ≤ .05. The largest statistic was *t*(53) = 6.62, FWE *p* = .0007, at MNI [-26, -102, -4] mm, well outside vmPFC. These global findings do not answer the vmPFC hypothesis and should not be interpreted as evidence for a gain effect in the target region.
![Whole-brain positive findings after max-T FWE correction](figures/whole_brain_fwe.png)

Each of the 54 supplied images is an unthresholded participant gain-effect estimate. The primary group model was a one-sample, voxelwise *t* test of these estimates against zero, testing the prespecified positive direction. We used 9,999 participant-level sign-flip permutations and the maximum *t* over the full brain mask for family-wise correction. This controls the whole-brain search, consistent with the original NARPS instruction to base the hypothesis decision on a whole-brain corrected analysis ([NARPS analysis instructions, Hypothesis 1](https://www.narps.info/files/narps_instructions_for_analysis_teams.pdf)).

We defined vmPFC before inspecting the group effects as a broad bilateral MNI search zone: |x| ≤ 20, y = 15 to 60, z = -20 to 10 mm. It captures ventral and medial prefrontal territory rather than a single focal coordinate. We used the [TemplateFlow MNI152NLin2009cAsym whole-brain mask](https://templateflow.s3.amazonaws.com/tpl-MNI152NLin2009cAsym/tpl-MNI152NLin2009cAsym_res-02_desc-brain_mask.nii.gz), nearest-neighbor resampled to the supplied map grid, intersected with voxels having nonzero estimates for all participants. The resulting search space had 186,192 voxels; 5,754 were in the vmPFC zone. The broad mask and independent whole-brain correction avoid treating an ROI-only or post hoc threshold as confirmatory evidence.

All 54 images had finite values and identical dimensions and affine; none was excluded. The shared mask excluded 11,837 voxels with common nonzero support that fell outside the template brain mask. Ages averaged 26.1 years (SD 3.0); metadata listed 30 women and 24 men. No demographic covariates were added to the intercept-only model.

The group result is absence of corrected support for a positive vmPFC effect, not proof that the neural effect is exactly zero. The descriptive interval is centered almost exactly on zero, but it is an interval for the mean of the supplied participant coefficients and is not an equivalence test. More importantly, participant variance maps were unavailable, so the group model could not weight first-level estimates by their individual uncertainty or separate that uncertainty from between-person variation. Sign-flip inference assumes a symmetric null distribution of participant effects.

A lack of support here means these group maps do not provide whole-brain-corrected evidence that larger potential gains produce a greater vmPFC response in this group under the stated model. It does not rule out smaller effects, effects under another valid first-level specification, or effects in a population beyond these 54 participants.

In the 54-person equal-indifference group, the positive gain-effect hypothesis was **not supported in vmPFC** by whole-brain family-wise-error (FWE) inference. The one-sided sign-flip max-t test found 24 significant positive voxels across the whole brain, but none fell in the bilateral AAL3 medial orbitofrontal parcels used to label vmPFC. The strongest whole-brain peak was posterior (MNI x = −26, y = −102, z = −3.6 mm; t = 6.62; max-t pFWE = 0.0008), outside the vmPFC hypothesis region. The other two small clusters were labeled inferior occipital cortex. These unanticipated locations do not support the vmPFC hypothesis.

The participant-average coefficient in the vmPFC parcels was −0.0079 model units (95% t interval −0.0346 to 0.0188). This summary is descriptive; the confirmatory decision is based on the whole-brain corrected map. Its peak vmPFC voxel was at (−2, 24, −13.2 mm; t = 2.34), with 0/1,297 vmPFC voxels passing max-t FWE at α = .05.

Each of the 54 supplied maps was treated as one participant’s gain coefficient from the fixed first-level model. We fit a one-sample random-effects group model, giving each participant equal weight because participant variance maps were not supplied. The directional alternative was a positive group effect, matching NARPS Hypothesis 1. To control family-wise error over the whole brain, we independently flipped each participant’s sign (5,000 permutations; seed 20261015), recalculated the t field, and compared each observed voxel with the permutation distribution of the maximum positive t across the common mask. The Monte Carlo p-value used the plus-one correction. This avoids selecting a vmPFC-only result after looking at the whole-brain data.

We defined the anatomical label using the bilateral AAL3 `Frontal_Med_Orb` parcels, which prior work maps to vmPFC. This is an explicit operational definition for a broad anatomical term, not a mask supplied by the task or the original teams. Parcels were used to locate and describe corrected findings; they did not provide a separate uncorrected confirmatory test. [NARPS specified a positive vmPFC gain effect for the equal-indifference group](https://www.narps.info/files/narps_instructions_for_analysis_teams.pdf); the AAL3 medial-orbital/vmPFC correspondence is described in [Rolls et al.](https://academic.oup.com/cercor/article/30/11/5830/5858256) and the [Nilearn AAL3 atlas documentation](https://nilearn.github.io/stable/modules/generated/nilearn.datasets.fetch_atlas_aal.html).

All 54 participant IDs matched the supplied cohort table; every map passed the manifest byte-count and SHA-256 checks. Maps shared a 97 × 115 × 81 grid, 2 × 2 × 2.4 mm voxel sizes, and matching affines; no non-finite values were found. Inference used the 198,029 voxels that were nonzero in every map, avoiding treating common zero padding as observed effects; the saved p-value map marks voxels outside this test mask as NaN. No participant was excluded. One participant (sub-025) was flagged by a robust outlier screen of the vmPFC parcel average and retained. Omitting that participant only for a sensitivity summary made the mean more negative (−0.0135; 95% interval −0.0382 to 0.0111), leaving the interpretation unchanged.

Failure to detect a corrected vmPFC effect means these supplied estimates do not provide whole-brain-corrected evidence for a positive vmPFC gain response in this group and model. It does **not** demonstrate that the true response is zero or rule out a smaller effect; the descriptive interval spans zero and no equivalence bound was specified. Positive corrected clusters elsewhere are not evidence for the hypothesized vmPFC location.

In the NARPS equal-indifference group, the supplied gain-modulator estimates do **not** provide whole-brain-corrected evidence that vmPFC response increases with potential gain. The primary test found no significant voxel in the prespecified anatomical vmPFC reference (peak within it: *t*(53) = 4.19, whole-brain *p*<sub>FWE</sub> = .801). The mean reference-region estimate was 0.0062 arbitrary units (95% *t* interval −0.0204 to 0.0327).

The whole-brain test did detect 24 positive voxels in three small occipital-pole clusters. The strongest voxel was at MNI (−26, −102, −3.6) mm, *t*(53) = 6.62, *p*<sub>FWE</sub> = .0008. These clusters are outside vmPFC and do not support the stated regional hypothesis. The original NARPS instructions specified a positive parametric gain effect in vmPFC for this group and required teams to report whole-brain analyses; we therefore used the full-brain corrected result for the hypothesis decision, not a vmPFC-only significance test ([NARPS analysis instructions](https://www.narps.info/files/narps_instructions_for_analysis_teams.pdf); see also the [NARPS methods paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7771346/)).

Family-wise error was controlled at .05 over 210,968 voxels by a maximum-*t* sign-flip permutation distribution (5,000 random sign flips; seed 20261015). Each sign was applied to a participant's full map, preserving the spatial dependence in that map; the maximum positive statistic across all tested voxels was used for each permutation. This is a one-sided test of the prespecified positive hypothesis, with the correction applied over the whole tested brain, following standard nonparametric neuroimaging inference ([Nichols & Holmes, 2002](https://doi.org/10.1002/hbm.1058)). The 95th percentile of the maximum-*t* null was 5.376.

All 54 supplied maps were included. They were finite and had matching dimensions and affine transforms (97 × 115 × 81; 2 × 2 × 2.4 mm). Coverage varied across maps, so the voxelwise group mask retained voxels with nonzero coverage in at least 90% of participants; this left 210,968 voxels. No participant was excluded. Metadata age and gender were not covariates in this one-group test. Available group-stage QC cannot revisit upstream motion or first-level fit diagnostics, which were not supplied with these maps.

We identified vmPFC independently of the activation results using the Harvard–Oxford cortical max-probability atlas (25% threshold), combining its “Frontal Medial Cortex” and “Subcallosal Cortex” labels and intersecting them with the group coverage mask (1,638 voxels). This broad anatomical reference was used for localization and a descriptive participant-level summary; it was not used to limit the primary test. The atlas is in MNI152NLin6Asym space and was nearest-neighbor resampled to the supplied MNI152NLin2009cAsym map grid. Atlas-to-template differences and the broadness of these labels limit anatomical precision ([FSL atlas format and labels](https://fsl.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/docs/other/atlas_xml.html)).

The data do not meet the prespecified whole-brain-corrected criterion for the vmPFC hypothesis. This is a lack of support at the chosen correction and sample size, not evidence that the true effect is exactly zero, that no participant shows a positive response, or that a practically relevant effect has been ruled out. The vmPFC mean interval includes both negative and positive values, and no equivalence margin was specified. The result also does not establish a unit-currency dose-response, because the first-level gain modulator was standardized. Positive whole-brain findings were small and localized to occipital pole; they are reported transparently but do not change the vmPFC conclusion.

**We found no support for a positive gain-related response in the vmPFC.** In the predefined bilateral medial orbitofrontal ROI, the mean participant cope was −0.0079 (95% t interval −0.0346 to 0.0188; 54 participants; descriptive one-sided t = −0.60, p = .723). No whole-brain FWE-significant voxel overlapped the ROI. The whole-brain max-t test detected 24 positive voxels in three small posterior patches (26-neighbor connectivity used for description only; peak t = 6.62 at MNI [−26, −102, −3.6]; minimum corrected p = .00050). These posterior findings do not support the vmPFC hypothesis.

We analyzed the 54 supplied equal-indifference participant maps; in this design, the potential gain range was twice the potential loss range. The input manifest checksums, byte counts, participant IDs, finite values, and common image geometry were verified before inference. No maps were excluded. A common-coverage whole-brain mask was defined as voxels with nonzero finite estimates in all 54 maps.

The primary model was a one-sample group test of the positive mean cope. Family-wise error was controlled across the whole common mask using a one-sided sign-flip permutation max-t test and 10,000 permutations (seed 20261015; α = .05). The hypothesis is supported only if the corrected map contains positive significant voxels in the vmPFC region. This follows the original NARPS instruction to report whole-brain analyses, not region-only tests ([NARPS analysis instructions](https://www.narps.info/files/narps_instructions_for_analysis_teams.pdf)).

The anatomical vmPFC summary used bilateral medial orbitofrontal parcels (`Frontal_Med_Orb_L/R`) from the AAL SPM12 atlas, resampled by nearest neighbor to the participant-map grid and intersected with common coverage. This is a fixed anatomical operationalization rather than a data-selected cluster. A published NARPS reanalysis similarly operationalized vmPFC with medial orbitofrontal parcels, while noting that the original hypothesis did not specify an atlas ROI ([NARPS analysis discussion](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10233921/)). We report the participants' average cope and t-based 95% interval descriptively; this ROI result does not replace whole-brain correction ([AAL atlas](https://doi.org/10.1006/nimg.2001.0978)).

No participant variance maps were supplied. The group test is an unweighted one-sample analysis of participant copes, not a precision-weighted mixed-effects model that propagates first-level uncertainty. Sign-flip inference also assumes exchangeability under sign changes (in particular, a sufficiently symmetric null distribution of participant effects). The 10,000 sampled permutations give Monte Carlo, not exhaustive, inference. A slower TFCE permutation attempt was interrupted for runtime; its duct logs are retained, and it is not used for the reported inference.

The absence of corrected vmPFC voxels means these data and this group model do not establish a positive gain effect in that region after whole-brain family-wise correction. It does not show that the effect is exactly zero or that vmPFC never tracks potential gains; smaller, spatially diffuse, or more variable effects may not be detected. The uncorrected ROI p-value is descriptive and is not evidence for or against the whole-brain-corrected hypothesis. Atlas boundaries and the MNI152-to-MNI2009cAsym resampling also make the ROI summary approximate.

We tested whether gain-related activity was positive in vmPFC in the 54-person equal-indifference group. The participant was the unit of analysis. We fit a one-sample group test of the supplied participant contrast estimates against zero, in the prespecified positive direction. Voxelwise family-wise error was controlled across the common participant support (198,029 voxels) with 5,000 participant-level sign flips and a maximum-t statistic (seed 20261016; minimum attainable Monte Carlo p = 0.00020).

We operationalized vmPFC as the union of Harvard-Oxford cortical atlas labels Frontal Medial Cortex, Subcallosal Cortex, Paracingulate Gyrus, and Frontal Orbital Cortex. This broad, prespecified mask contributed 6,174 tested voxels after nearest-neighbor resampling. Since vmPFC has no single agreed anatomical boundary, the mask is an explicit working definition. Support required a positive voxel inside it to pass the same whole-brain FWE p < .05 threshold; the ROI average below is descriptive and does not replace that criterion.

No positive vmPFC voxel survived whole-brain correction (0 of 6,174 mask voxels). The descriptive mean participant estimate within the mask was −0.0103 (95% t interval −0.0290 to 0.0084; t(53) = −1.10; one-sided p = .862); 21 of 54 participant averages were positive. Leave-one-participant-out ROI means ranged from −0.0144 to −0.0076. These data do not support the predicted positive vmPFC response.

There were 24 positive voxels surviving whole-brain correction elsewhere. The strongest was at MNI [−26, −102, −3.6] mm (mean estimate 0.1121, t = 6.62, max-t FWE p = .0010), outside the vmPFC mask. This finding does not support the vmPFC-specific hypothesis.

This is a lack of corrected evidence for the hypothesized positive vmPFC response, not evidence that the true response is exactly zero or that smaller effects are absent. The ROI interval includes zero and modest positive values. The inference depends on sign-flip exchangeability and approximately symmetric participant errors; the one-sided maximum-t correction is conservative and voxelwise. The vmPFC anatomy is broad and atlas-dependent. Harvard-Oxford uses MNI152 2-mm geometry and was nearest-neighbor resampled to MNI152NLin2009cAsym, so small registration differences can affect ROI boundaries; the corrected positive peak is far posterior to this mask.

The inputs are unthresholded AO86 participant contrast parameter estimates, not standardized statistics or group results. Upstream gain regressors were mean-centered and variance-normalized before HRF convolution, so these coefficients cannot be read as change per currency unit. The provided effects come from a gain model separate from the loss model and are conditional on that choice. Because participant variance maps and the executable first-level workflow were not supplied, this analysis cannot use first-level uncertainty for precision-weighted mixed-effects inference; the group test uses between-participant variation in the supplied estimates. No time-series scans or upstream processing were rerun.

All 54 listed participants were included; no maps failed checksum, geometry, or finite-value checks, and no exclusions were made. The common-support rule, input checksums, atlas mask, voxelwise maps, permutation maxima, and machine-readable summary are retained with the outputs.

Does greater potential gain elicit a greater fMRI response in ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) in the NARPS equal-indifference group? **This analysis did not find whole-brain-corrected support for a positive vmPFC effect.** A one-sided whole-brain test found 23 positive voxels elsewhere, in bilateral posterior occipital locations (approximately MNI x = −28 to +32, y = −104 to −94, z = −8.4 to −1.2 mm). None were in the vmPFC search region. The largest statistic was t(53) = 6.62 at (−26, −102, −3.6), max-t familywise p = .0007; that posterior location does not support the vmPFC hypothesis.

We analyzed the 54 supplied equal-indifference participant maps (one observation per participant) using an intercept-only one-sample group model. The target was the population mean participant gain-effect estimate at each voxel; the directional alternative was mean > 0. The effect maps are upstream contrast parameter estimates, not t or z statistics. AO86 normalized the gain modulator before HRF convolution, so coefficients are not change per currency unit. Gains and losses were modeled separately. The supplied maps average four runs; preprocessing and individual models were treated as fixed.

We tested 196,120 voxels in the common MNI152 brain mask, resampled to the input grid (2 × 2 × 2.4 mm). Whole-brain familywise error was controlled using 9,999 participant-level sign flips and the maximum positive one-sample t statistic (seed 20261015; one-sided alpha = .05). Sign flipping assumes independent participants and sign-symmetric null errors. The maps and code are available in this repository; the plan and fixed upstream methods are in [`analysis-plan.md`](../protocol/analysis-plan.md) and [`upstream-methods.md`](../input/upstream-methods.md).

Because vmPFC has no single universally agreed atlas boundary, we used an explicit MNI coordinate search box for descriptive summaries: |x| ≤ 10, 20 ≤ y ≤ 60, and −20 ≤ z ≤ 20 mm. This identifies an anterior midline ventral prefrontal swath; it is not an atlas-derived ROI, and it was not used to reduce the multiple-comparison family. We also checked the corrected voxel coordinates directly: all lie far posterior to vmPFC. Thus the regional conclusion does not depend on a marginal boundary decision around the search box.

All 54 participant maps passed checksum, geometry, and finite-value checks; there were no exclusions. The descriptive mean effect in the vmPFC coordinate box was −0.0022 map units (between-participant SD 0.071; 95% t interval for the mean [−0.0215, 0.0172]). The interval spans zero and the mean is close to zero. The whole-mask participant average was −0.0070 map units (95% t interval [−0.0215, 0.0075]); this is descriptive and does not replace voxelwise inference. Both summaries use supplied normalized-modulator estimates, not effects per currency unit. A post-selection check at the voxel with the largest observed vmPFC-box t statistic found t(53) = 4.19, uncorrected one-sided p = 5.3 × 10⁻⁵, but max-t FWE p = .791. Selecting the maximum within the box makes the uncorrected value optimistic; the corrected result does not support a regional claim. As a sensitivity analysis, voxelwise Bonferroni correction identified 11 positive voxels across the brain and zero in vmPFC, consistent with the primary max-t result.

The corrected positive foci were posterior and bilateral, not vmPFC. Their presence does not rescue the vmPFC hypothesis. The independent numerical checks recomputed one-sample t statistics at 20 sampled voxels, directly reconstructed 20 sign-flip maxima, reconstructed the full voxelwise FWE p map and both threshold maps, verified checksums and geometry, and rebuilt the vmPFC, selected-voxel, global-average, and Bonferroni summaries from participant maps; all passed ([validation log](../logs/20261016T-final-validation2info.json)).

The result is **lack of support under this group model and supplied contrast**, not evidence that the true vmPFC effect is exactly zero. The interval is not an equivalence test, and voxelwise non-significance can reflect limited precision or power. No participant-level variance maps were supplied, so the model weights participants equally and cannot account for different first-level estimation precision. The gain regressor was normalized, and gain and loss were modeled in separate upstream models; the estimates cannot isolate currency-scaled gain sensitivity from every task-design dependency. In this task version the gain range was twice the loss range, so this analysis also does not establish how neural response scales compare across gain and loss ranges. These maps alone cannot resolve those questions.

# Potential gains and vmPFC activity

**This analysis does not support a positive gain effect in vmPFC after whole-brain correction.** The complete equal-indifference cohort (54 participants) was analyzed with a one-sided, one-sample group test on the supplied participant gain-effect maps. No voxel in the anatomically defined vmPFC region survived whole-brain family-wise error correction. The highest-t vmPFC voxel was at MNI (−2, 24, −18), t(53)=4.19, but its whole-brain max-t adjusted p was .782.

The descriptive mean across the vmPFC ROI was 0.012 cope units (95% t interval −0.008 to 0.033; one-sided unadjusted p=.115). Participants varied around that mean. This interval is compatible with small negative and positive average effects; it is not an equivalence test and does not establish a zero effect.

The whole-brain test found 24 voxels with positive effects at max-t FWE p≤.05. The maximum was posterior cerebellar (MNI −26, −102, −3.6; t(53)=6.62; FWE p=.0007), outside vmPFC. This corrected result does not support the vmPFC-specific hypothesis.
![Participant vmPFC effects and 95% t interval](results/group-analysis/vmPFC_effects.png)
![Whole-brain positive effects surviving max-t FWE correction; cyan outline shows the independent vmPFC anatomical ROI](results/group-analysis/whole_brain_fwe.png)

The primary test was a one-sided, voxelwise one-sample t statistic calibrated by 9,999 random participant sign flips. Each permutation’s maximum positive t over the common coverage mask formed the null distribution, controlling family-wise error at α=.05 across voxels supported in every participant. The seed was 20261015. The union support included 251,063 voxels, but exact-zero support differed across maps at 53,034 voxels. The final mask uses the all-participant nonzero intersection (198,029 voxels), avoiding treating unsupported zeros as observed effects. Because no separate participant brain masks were supplied, this may also omit valid exact-zero estimates near coverage edges. No participants were excluded. Input image geometry matched, all 54 map identities matched the pinned cohort table, and the analysis verified input SHA256 checksums.

To interpret vmPFC anatomically without restricting the primary whole-brain search, we used the union of Harvard–Oxford cortical `Frontal Orbital Cortex` and `Subcallosal Cortex` probability values ≥25%, limited to |x|≤15 mm, y≥0, and z≤0 in MNI coordinates. The ROI contains 797 voxels in common participant support. This is a transparent operational definition of orbitomedial/subcallosal vmPFC; boundaries vary across atlases. The supplied maps use MNI152NLin2009cAsym, while Harvard–Oxford and the display template use standard MNI152, so ROI boundaries and coordinates are approximate. Atlas and template files are locally pinned with checksums. [Harvard–Oxford atlas documentation](https://nilearn.github.io/stable/modules/generated/nilearn.datasets.fetch_atlas_harvard_oxford.html).

The original NARPS instructions asked teams to judge their hypotheses from whole-brain corrected results rather than an ROI-only test; the NARPS paper describes that reporting requirement and the cross-team variability it produced. This analysis therefore treats a corrected voxel within vmPFC as the relevant evidence, and reports the ROI average only as a descriptive estimate. [Original NARPS analysis instructions](https://www.narps.info/files/narps_instructions_for_analysis_teams.pdf); [NARPS analysis-variability paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2314-9).

The maps are AO86 participant contrast parameter estimates averaged over four runs, not standardized statistics or group estimates. The upstream gain modulator was mean-centered and variance-normalized before HRF convolution, so these coefficients are not BOLD change per dollar. Gain and loss were modeled separately, making this effect conditional on that upstream specification. No participant variance maps or complete executable participant pipeline were supplied; the group analysis could not model first-level precision and gives each participant equal weight. Sign-flip inference assumes independent participant effects and a symmetric null distribution. Failure to detect corrected vmPFC support means this analysis did not establish the predicted effect; it does not show that vmPFC has no gain response.
